title: BERT Loses Patience: Fast and Robust Inference with Early Exit (PABEE)
abstract: Adds inexpensive classification exits to every layer of BERT and stops inference early via a patience rule (k consecutive agreeing predictions), so easy inputs exit early and hard ones run deeper, cutting compute with little accuracy loss.
oneLiner: Patience-based early exit for encoder transformers that waits for k agreeing predictions before stopping.
keyFinding: Patience-based exits remain robust to noisy intermediate predictions, saving significant FLOPs with minimal accuracy loss and beating confidence-only early exits.
weakness: Encoder-only and classification-centric; not designed for decoder-only, long-context generative LLMs or token-level decoding.
implication: The exit decision is input-dependent, so per-input compute is unequal (a seed of the fairness concern).
relevance: Establishes the foundational input-conditional-compute mechanism that can allocate fewer layers to 'easy' (possibly group-skewed) inputs.

title: DeeBERT: Dynamic Early Exiting for Accelerating BERT Inference
abstract: Inserts lightweight classifiers into intermediate BERT layers and exits per sample when confidence exceeds a threshold, accelerating inference while largely preserving accuracy.
oneLiner: Confidence-threshold early exit via intermediate output heads.
keyFinding: Early exits cut computation substantially with a small accuracy drop, but only after fine-tuning the internal classifiers and tuning a global threshold.
weakness: Requires fine-tuning (not plug-in); hard global threshold; classification only.
implication: The threshold that decides compute spend is tuned globally on aggregate accuracy, so any group with lower confidence is handled differently.
relevance: Illustrates that the threshold deciding compute spend is global, so systematically lower-confidence inputs get more compute (or are cut off and misclassified).

title: FastBERT: A Self-distilling BERT with Adaptive Inference Time
abstract: Adds classifier branches at each layer and lets each sample stop at a different depth, with self-distillation so intermediate representations are supervised toward the final output.
oneLiner: Sample-adaptive inference where each layer has a classifier branch and samples exit at different depths.
keyFinding: Self-distillation makes intermediate predictions informative enough for early exits to mirror final-layer behavior, enabling large speedups with minimal loss.
weakness: Encoder-only/classification; branch confidence can be mis-calibrated; no generation.
implication: Because compute is input-dependent and driven by self-distilled confidence, any confidence bias transfers into compute-allocation bias.
relevance: Shows adaptive compute is driven by self-distilled confidence, so biased confidence across groups directly biases compute allocation.

title: Confident Adaptive Language Modeling (CALM)
abstract: For decoder-only next-token LMs, CALM dynamically chooses how many layers to run per token based on softmax confidence, with a risk-controlling formulation bounding the probability of premature stopping.
oneLiner: Per-token adaptive depth for generative LLMs, exiting when the current layer's softmax confidence is high enough.
keyFinding: CALM terminates most tokens after a few layers while matching full-depth quality, using a risk-controlling threshold with statistical guarantees.
weakness: Threshold tuning on English corpora; per-token exits complicate KV-cache and batch GPU utilization; no group-wise analysis.
implication: Every token's compute depends on the model's self-reported confidence, directly redistributing work per token.
relevance: The canonical LLM early-exit method; its per-token confidence-driven depth allocation is exactly the mechanism that could deliver unequal compute to groups.

title: A Simple Hash-Based Early Exiting Approach For Language Understanding and Generation
abstract: Uses a cheap hash function over token embeddings to decide early exit for each token, making early exiting nearly free and applicable to both understanding and generation.
oneLiner: A training-free, hash-based early-exit controller keyed on the token itself rather than learned confidence.
keyFinding: A simple token hash is surprisingly competitive, showing much of the speedup comes from skipping layers on predictable tokens rather than sophisticated confidence estimators.
weakness: Coarse, uncertainty-agnostic signal; brittle across domains; no subgroup evaluation.
implication: The exit signal being a function of token identity means compute allocation is purely a function of surface token, independent of model confidence.
relevance: Shows the exit decision need not rely on model confidence, sharpening the point that any input-dependent policy can yield unequal group compute.

title: SkipDecode: Autoregressive Skip Decoding with Batching and Caching for Efficient LLM Inference
abstract: Builds a per-layer skip decision during autoregressive decoding while remaining compatible with KV-cache batching, making layer skipping practical in batched LLM serving.
oneLiner: A system-oriented early-exit method that makes layer skipping practical in batched, KV-cached LLM inference.
keyFinding: Layer skipping can be made batching- and caching-friendly, unlocking real wall-clock decode speedups in a serving stack, not just FLOPs savings.
weakness: Heuristic/confidence per-token skip decisions; quality can degrade on hard tokens; gains depend on batch composition.
implication: In batched serving, per-token skip decisions determine per-token GPU work, and batch composition shapes achievable speedup.
relevance: Bridges early-exit research to serving practice, showing how compute is reallocated per token in batched decode where fairness of allocation matters.

title: Mixture-of-Depths: Dynamically allocating compute in transformer-based language models
abstract: Routes each token through a variable number of transformer blocks via a learned top-k selection of which tokens occupy a block at each layer, allocating compute dynamically during training and inference.
oneLiner: A routing-based scheme where each layer processes only a top-k subset of tokens, dynamically allocating compute per token.
keyFinding: Models can learn which tokens deserve more compute; capacity-based MoD matches or beats dense quality while using much fewer FLOPs per token.
weakness: Routing is by capacity/FLOPs not correctness on hard samples; optimizer-sensitive; not a decode-time confidence exit.
implication: Token-level routing is learned, so which tokens receive more compute is an emergent, trainable property, potentially correlated with token frequency/domain.
relevance: Key alternative to confidence exits: a learned router allocates compute per token, raising the same fairness-of-allocation question.

title: Mixture-of-Recursions: Learning Dynamic Recursive Depths for Adaptive Token-Level Computation
abstract: Scaling LLMs is expensive. Existing efficiency efforts target either parameter sharing or adaptive computation, but rarely both. Mixture-of-Recursions (MoR) combines both axes in a single Recursive Transformer: it reuses a shared stack of layers across recursion steps for parameter efficiency while lightweight routers adaptively assign different recursion depths to individual tokens (adaptive token-level thinking), focusing quadratic attention only among still-active tokens and caching only their KV pairs. A KV-sharing variant reuses KV pairs from the first recursion to cut memory. Across 135M-1.7B scales, MoR forms a new Pareto frontier, lowering validation perplexity and improving few-shot accuracy at equal training FLOPs while boosting throughput vs. vanilla/recursive baselines.
oneLiner: Per-token depth routing boosts efficiency and quality but is trained without any group-fairness awareness.
keyFinding: MoR sets a new Pareto frontier at 135M-1.7B scale: lower perplexity and better few-shot accuracy at equal FLOPs with higher throughput.
weakness: Purely efficiency/quality; no fairness dimension, no demographic analysis, no per-group allocation audit; routers trained on loss, not equity.
implication: The mechanism that d1 must scrutinize — per-token/instance compute allocation — is now a trained router, so any group-correlation in that allocation is learned and thus auditable.
relevance: C. Background mechanism; makes the adaptive-allocation object concrete but contains no fairness analysis.
whyLatest: Jul 2025 (window edge). Represents the current state of per-token adaptive depth allocation.
novelty: Unifies parameter sharing and adaptive computation; learns per-token recursive depths with lightweight routers and selective KV caching.

title: Dynamic layer selection in decoder-only transformers
abstract: Trains a routing mechanism that selects a variable subset of decoder-only transformer layers to run per input, so different inputs use different effective depths.
oneLiner: Learned per-input routing over decoder layers, activating a different subset per sample.
keyFinding: A small learned router can predict which layers an input needs without retraining the backbone, yielding compute savings with limited quality loss.
weakness: Router trained per task/domain; coarse layer selection; no subpopulation analysis.
implication: Which layers run is a learned function of the input, making compute budget a learned, input-dependent quantity.
relevance: Demonstrates a learned exit/router policy for LLMs whose input-dependent decisions are exactly what would need fairness auditing.

title: Depth-Adaptive Transformer
abstract: Proposes depth-adaptive computation in Transformers, letting each input decide how many layers to use (early exit) to reduce computation while preserving quality.
oneLiner: Per-example depth-adaptive inference: each input exits at its own best depth.
keyFinding: Combining per-example halting/classifiers with layer-specific classifiers lets models stop early on easy inputs while preserving quality on hard ones.
weakness: Efficiency-focused; fairness across groups not analyzed.
implication: Because exit depth is chosen per example, if accuracy-vs-depth curves differ across groups, exiting is not fairness-neutral.
relevance: Establishes depth-adaptive inference as an efficiency method whose per-input depth choice can amplify group differences if maturity differs by group.

title: The Right Tool for the Job: Matching Model and Instance Complexities
abstract: Shows that NLP models can adapt computation to input complexity, routing easier instances to smaller models and harder ones to deeper models.
oneLiner: Different examples need different compute, so adaptive depth beats one fixed model.
keyFinding: A complexity estimator/router sends light outputs for easy instances and deep computation for hard ones, improving the efficiency-accuracy frontier.
weakness: No demographic-fairness analysis; relies on complexity measures that may correlate with group.
implication: If complexity (and hence chosen depth) correlates with a demographic group, early-exit routing produces group-skewed accuracy.
relevance: Demonstrates early-exit depth is chosen per instance, so group differences in maturity yield unequal accuracy.

title: Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding
abstract: Introduces speculative decoding: a small draft model proposes tokens that a larger target model verifies in parallel, giving 2-3x wall-clock speedups while provably preserving the exact output distribution.
oneLiner: Use a small draft model to guess tokens, then verify them in parallel with the big model for exact-distribution speedups.
keyFinding: Speculative decoding achieves 2-3x faster decoding while provably producing the identical output distribution as the target model.
weakness: Requires a matching draft model plus extra memory; speedup collapses when draft and target distributions diverge.
implication: Because sampling quality is preserved exactly, this form of acceleration does not itself alter model behavior.
relevance: Demonstrates lossless acceleration; early-exit fairness work must justify why its quality/fairness trade-offs are acceptable when lossless options exist.

title: Medusa: Simple LLM Inference Acceleration Framework with Multiple Decoding Heads
abstract: Adds multiple parallel decoding heads on top of a frozen base LLM to predict several future tokens at once, combined with tree-based attention and typical-acceptance sampling, with no separate draft model.
oneLiner: Add parallel prediction heads to the base model so several tokens are guessed and verified in one step.
keyFinding: Medusa delivers ~2.2x decoding speedup on Vicuna-7B/33B and 2.3x on MT-Bench while preserving quality, with no extra draft model.
weakness: Requires training/alignment of heads; speedup bounded by acceptance rates.
implication: A model can predict its own future tokens with auxiliary heads, avoiding the extra-draft-model cost.
relevance: Shows a model-specific accelerator can change token distributions; such output shifts need auditing across demographic groups.

title: EAGLE: Speculative Sampling Requires Rethinking Feature Uncertainty
abstract: EAGLE drafts autoregressively in the feature (hidden-state) space rather than token space, conditioning on the target model's feature distribution to lower uncertainty and raise acceptance, achieving 2-3x and up to 5x latency reduction.
oneLiner: Draft in the hidden-feature space instead of token space to make draft predictions far more accurate.
keyFinding: Feature-level drafting sharply raises acceptance rates, giving ~2-3x latency reduction (up to 5x in some settings) while strictly preserving the output distribution.
weakness: Draft header must be retrained per base model; adds memory/complexity.
implication: The space in which you draft (features vs tokens) is a dominant factor in speculative-decoding efficiency.
relevance: Highlights that this acceleration family's ceiling is draft precision, which matters when auditing whether acceleration changes output behavior.

title: LayerSkip: Enabling Early Exit Inference and Self-Speculative Decoding
abstract: Trains LLMs with layer dropout plus early-exit loss so they can exit at intermediate layers; at inference these exits either provide direct early-exit output or serve as a draft for self-speculative decoding verified by the full model.
oneLiner: Jointly optimizes LLMs to (1) exit early and (2) feed an early-exit draft to the full model for lossless self-speculative decoding.
keyFinding: Combining layer dropout with early-exit self-distillation lets a single model both accelerate via early exit and accelerate losslessly via self-speculation.
weakness: Requires a customized training recipe; early-exit and draft quality both depend on training; decoder-only; exit adds serving complexity.
implication: The early-exit head is both a quality-critical decision point and the draft source, so its confidence behavior drives both speed and correctness.
relevance: State-of-the-art early-exit + self-speculative LLM method; ideal target for measuring per-token compute/correctness differences across groups.

title: Draft & Verify: Lossless Large Language Model Acceleration via Self-Speculative Decoding
abstract: Proposes self-speculative decoding: the same LLM drafts tokens by exiting early from an intermediate layer, then verifies them with its full forward pass, yielding lossless acceleration without a separate draft model.
oneLiner: Lossless self-speculative decoding where an early exit acts as the draft model and the full model verifies.
keyFinding: An early-exit draft from the same model can be verified by the full model to give exact match with baseline output while speeding up decoding.
weakness: Draft quality and speedup depend on early-exit accuracy; draft-verify complicates serving; speedup varies by input; no fairness analysis.
implication: Decode speed and correctness hinge on the early-exit draft, so tokens drafted/accepted differently across groups affect both cost and quality.
relevance: Gives a clean, quantifiable signal (acceptance rate per input) for detecting unequal compute allocation while keeping outputs correct.

title: Kangaroo: Lossless Self-Speculative Decoding via Double Early Exiting
abstract: Uses a lightweight self-drafting mechanism with two early-exit stages — a cheap draft exit and a verification/proposal stage — to accelerate lossless decoding within a single model.
oneLiner: Double early exiting within one model to draft and verify tokens losslessly for faster decoding.
keyFinding: Combining a cheap early-exit draft with a second, more reliable intermediate verification improves acceptance rate and speedup while keeping output lossless.
weakness: Adds architectural complexity (multiple exits); requires intermediate-state access; no fairness/group analysis of accept rate or latency.
implication: The double-exit design allocates compute across two decision points per token, again making compute a token-level predicted quantity.
relevance: Represents the trend toward increasingly fine-grained, model-internal exit policies, the surface where fairness-of-computation should be audited.

title: GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers
abstract: GPTQ is a one-shot weight quantization method based on approximate second-order information that compresses LLM weights to 3-4 bits while preserving accuracy.
oneLiner: Compress LLM weights to 3-4 bits with a Hessian-based method that keeps accuracy nearly intact.
keyFinding: GPTQ compresses LLMs to 3-4 bits per weight with only a small perplexity increase, giving 2-3x faster inference.
weakness: Upfront second-order computation is costly; weight-only (activations stay high precision); results depend on calibration data.
implication: Post-training quantization can be near-lossless for LLMs without retraining.
relevance: Low-bit weight compression interacts with the layers an early-exit system keeps, so per-group accuracy auditing is relevant.

title: AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration
abstract: AWQ identifies a small set of salient weight channels by observing activation magnitudes rather than weight magnitudes, then protects those channels during quantization.
oneLiner: Guard a few important weight channels, found by activation magnitude, to get high-quality low-bit quantization.
keyFinding: AWQ quantizes to 4-bit with much better accuracy than prior methods and enables on-device Llama serving with 3x+ speedups and large memory savings.
weakness: Requires validation-set activation statistics; saliency is per-model; overhead to find salient channels.
implication: Activation statistics, not raw weight magnitudes, determine which weights need protecting in quantization.
relevance: Shows quantization choices are activation-driven; analogous activation-based checks matter for fairness auditing of early-exit systems.

title: SparseGPT: Massive Language Models Can Be Accurately Pruned in One-Shot
abstract: SparseGPT prunes massive LLMs to 50-60% sparsity in a single shot using a scalable layer-wise method that reformulates pruning as sparse regression, with almost no accuracy loss and no retraining.
oneLiner: Prune giant LLMs down to half their weights in one shot using a scalable sparse-regression method.
keyFinding: SparseGPT removes 50-60% of weights from models up to 175B in one shot with near-zero accuracy loss, without retraining.
weakness: Mostly unstructured sparsity needing specialized hardware for speed; Hessian cost high; accuracy drops at very high sparsity.
implication: Post-training pruning can yield large weight reduction without retraining, but real speed requires hardware support.
relevance: Pruning changes which weights survive; resulting output differences across demographic groups could be audited for fairness.

title: LLM-Pruner: On the Structural Pruning of Large Language Models
abstract: LLM-Pruner performs structural pruning of LLMs by removing coupled structures (attention heads, FFN channels) selected by gradient-based importance in a task-agnostic way, then lightly fine-tunes to recover performance.
oneLiner: Prune whole structures such as heads and channels using gradient importance, then recover with light fine-tuning.
keyFinding: Structural pruning reduces LLaMA-7B to ~2.7B-equivalent FLOPs with only modest loss in zero-shot accuracy.
weakness: Requires fine-tuning recovery; instruction-following degrades; quality loss not zero.
implication: Real hardware speed/memory gains require structural (not just unstructured) pruning, which costs some accuracy.
relevance: Removing attention heads or depth layers changes which language patterns are preserved, directly relevant to fairness auditing.

title: H2O: Heavy-Hitter Oracle for Efficient Generative Inference of Large Language Models
abstract: H2O introduces an attention KV-cache eviction policy that keeps a small set of frequently-attended 'heavy-hitter' tokens plus recent tokens, reducing cache memory by up to 20x and improving throughput while maintaining quality.
oneLiner: Keep only the frequently-attended 'heavy-hitter' tokens plus recent ones to shrink the KV cache dramatically.
keyFinding: H2O cuts KV-cache memory by up to 20x and boosts throughput while keeping or improving generation quality.
weakness: Heuristic importance measure; may drop tokens critical for long-context reasoning, so quality can degrade on some tasks.
implication: Not all past tokens matter equally; attention-based selection can greatly reduce memory without much accuracy loss.
relevance: KV eviction decides which context is remembered; which tokens get dropped could differ across demographic groups.

title: Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks
abstract: StreamingLLM observes that streaming LLMs need 'attention sinks' (a few initial tokens) to stabilize attention, combining them with a rolling window to enable stable inference over millions of tokens with constant memory.
oneLiner: Keep a few initial 'sink' tokens in the KV cache so attention stays stable over millions of generated tokens.
keyFinding: Attention sinks plus a local sliding window let LLMs stream over more than 4M tokens with constant memory and no quality collapse.
weakness: Performance depends on sink curation; limited to very long streaming contexts.
implication: KV-cache memory can be made constant even for unbounded generation by retaining a minimal set of sink tokens.
relevance: Shows attention module behavior can be strongly shaped by a few retained tokens, relevant to how context is parameterized and audited.

title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
abstract: FlashAttention is an IO-aware exact attention algorithm that computes attention in tiles without materializing the large intermediate attention matrix, using recomputation to cut memory and improve wall-clock speed.
oneLiner: Compute exact attention in tiles, never writing the full attention matrix to HBM, so it is faster and far more memory-efficient.
keyFinding: FlashAttention delivers 2-4x wall-clock speedup and large memory savings, enabling much longer sequence lengths (refined in FlashAttention-2).
weakness: Optimized for GPU HBM/BF16; gains hardware-specific; an implementation improvement, not a change to attention math.
implication: A large part of achievable attention speedup is an I/O and memory-efficiency problem rather than an algorithmic one.
relevance: Attention-serving efficiency is the baseline every early-exit and dynamic-depth method is compared against.

title: The Unreasonable Ineffectiveness of the Deeper Layers
abstract: Shows that many of the deepest layers of trained LLMs contribute negligibly at inference, and that dropping them with a cheap layer-selection heuristic preserves performance while enabling faster inference (and sometimes improving tasks like MMLU).
oneLiner: Many of an LLM's deepest layers hardly matter, so you can drop them at inference for a nearly-free speedup.
keyFinding: Dropping roughly half the deepest layers of a 70B model gives ~1.5x speedup on a consumer GPU with minimal performance loss; some tasks like MMLU improve.
weakness: Task-dependent; can hurt reasoning/math; simple heuristic selection not always optimal.
implication: Depth-wise redundancy can be exploited for inference-time early exit at nearly zero cost.
relevance: Directly relevant to early exit: deciding which layers to drop determines the output changes that must be audited for demographic fairness.

title: BBQ: A Hand-Built Bias Benchmark for Question Answering
abstract: BBQ is a QA benchmark of ~25k questions across nine social-bias categories, each in disambiguated and ambiguous contexts, scoring whether models rely on stereotypes when the answer is not inferable.
oneLiner: A hand-built QA benchmark measuring how strongly LLMs lean on demographic stereotypes by contrasting disambiguated vs ambiguous settings.
keyFinding: Large pretrained QA models show substantial bias in ambiguous contexts (often worse than majority/random baselines), expressed as a large accuracy gap between stereotypic and non-stereotypic answers.
weakness: English QA templates; limited context; ambiguous/abstract items hard to scale.
implication: A model can look 'fair' on unambiguous inputs yet be strongly biased when information is missing, so fairness must be measured in under-determined settings.
relevance: Its accuracy-gap and bias-score framing is the closest template for testing whether an early-exit/adaptive LLM yields unequal QA accuracy across groups.

title: BOLD: Dataset and Metrics for Measuring Biases in Open-Ended Language Generation
abstract: BOLD is a dataset of 23,679 English Wikipedia prompt templates over five domains (gender, race, religion, political affiliation, profession) with five fairness metrics — sentiment, regard, toxicity, gender polarity, word-level similarity.
oneLiner: A large open-ended generation benchmark with concrete per-domain fairness metrics to quantify bias in LLM output text.
keyFinding: Larger models (GPT-2, GPT-3) display more bias in sentiment, regard, and toxicity toward specific groups than smaller ones, with direction/intensity depending on domain.
weakness: Metrics lean on external classifiers with measurement error; coreference/regard judgments can misattribute group sentiment.
implication: Scaling up models is not bias-neutral; quality and 'fairness' signals must be tracked by group during generation.
relevance: Supplies per-group sentiment/regard/toxicity metrics to compare whether early-exit LLMs degrade output quality differently across groups.

title: Gender Bias in Coreference Resolution: Evaluation and Debiasing Methods
abstract: Introduces WinoBias, a coreference-resolution dataset built around stereotypical and anti-stereotypical profession/pronoun pairs to expose gender bias, plus two debiasing methods (gender-balanced embeddings and data augmentation).
oneLiner: The canonical gendered coreference benchmark revealing a large performance gap on stereotypical vs anti-stereotypical examples.
keyFinding: Coreference systems perform far worse on anti-stereotypical sentences; data augmentation and gender-balanced embeddings narrow but do not remove the gap.
weakness: Binary-gender framing; English profession/pronoun stimuli; train/test distribution mismatch can inflate apparent bias.
implication: A model's reliability is not uniform across demographic groups — performance can be tied to stereotype conformance.
relevance: A classic template for measuring an accuracy/quality disparity between demographic groups — the kind that adaptive inference could introduce or amplify.

title: RealToxicityPrompts: Evaluating Neural Toxic Degeneration in Language Models
abstract: RealToxicityPrompts is a dataset of 100k naturally occurring web prompts whose continuations are scored for toxicity via the Perspective API, documenting 'toxic degeneration' and evaluating filtering, detoxification, and decoding strategies as mitigation.
oneLiner: The standard dataset and framework for measuring and reducing toxic/unsafe outputs in open-ended generation.
keyFinding: Pretrained LMs readily produce toxic continuations from fairly neutral prompts, and toxicity rises with generation length and model size; mitigations reduce but do not eliminate it.
weakness: Toxicity measured by a single external classifier that can itself be biased; prompts are single English web snippets.
implication: Inference-time choices (length, decoding, caching) materially change the risk-profile of generated content, so adaptive inference can shift harm.
relevance: Shows inference-time behavior (which early-exit changes) alters harm; a natural outcome variable for measuring uneven quality/harm across demographics.

title: StereoSet: Measuring stereotypical bias in pretrained language models
abstract: StereoSet measures stereotypical bias using intrasentence and intersentence contexts across gender, race, religion, and profession, defining a StereoSet Score combining stereotype preference with a language-modeling score.
oneLiner: Introduces the StereoSet Score to quantify a pretrained LM's preference for stereotypical associations while accounting for fluency.
keyFinding: Pretrained models exhibit substantial stereotype preference, and in several cases it increases with model scale/capability.
weakness: Associational (co-occurrence-based) measure that can conflate statistical correlation with genuinely harmful bias; limited to four domains.
implication: Bigger, more capable models are not automatically fairer; bias can scale with capability, so capability gains must be audited separately.
relevance: The stereotype-preference metric is a direct handle for testing whether an early-exit LLM emits more stereotypical completions when computation is budgeted.

title: CrowS-Pairs: A Challenge Dataset for Measuring Social Biases in Masked Language Models
abstract: CrowS-Pairs is a benchmark of 1,508 minimal sentence pairs (one stereotypical, one anti-stereotypical) across nine bias categories, scored by the relative likelihood a masked LM assigns to the stereotypical sentence.
oneLiner: A minimal-pair benchmark scoring social bias by comparing model likelihood of stereotypical vs anti-stereotypical sentences.
keyFinding: All tested pretrained masked LMs show measurable social bias favoring stereotypical sentences, with magnitude varying by category and model.
weakness: Relies on likelihood differences that engineers can game; sentence-level and English-only; sensitive to template wording.
implication: Bias is present even in models not explicitly designed for generation, and is a property of learned associations, not just decode-time choices.
relevance: A lightweight group-bias probe adaptable to checking whether early-exit thresholds alter the relative likelihood of stereotypical completions.

title: A Group Fairness Lens for Large Language Models
abstract: Proposes a group-level fairness framework for LLMs evaluating fairness by comparing the distribution/quality of outputs across demographic groups rather than by a single scalar, arguing group-based comparison reveals disparities masked by pooled scores.
oneLiner: Argues for measuring LLM fairness at the group level across outputs, not with a single aggregate number.
keyFinding: LLMs exhibit measurable group-level disparities in generated-output quality/content that are hidden when only a single pooled fairness value is reported.
weakness: Group definitions and output-level metric choices are modeler-defined; limited to text-generation outputs and English settings.
implication: Reporting only an average fairness score can conceal systematic disadvantage to specific demographic groups.
relevance: Directly supplies the group-disparity evaluation lens to decide whether early-exit LLMs allocate different quality across demographic groups.

title: Measuring Social Biases in Masked Language Models by Proxy of Prediction Quality
abstract: Proposes measuring social bias in masked LMs through per-group prediction quality (accuracy/confidence on tokens associated with different social groups) rather than only through likelihood preference.
oneLiner: Frames bias as a differential in prediction quality/accuracy across social groups, not just association likelihood.
keyFinding: Models show differential prediction quality across demographic group tokens, revealing an accuracy/confidence gap tied to group identity that pure preference measures can miss.
weakness: Requires careful token/group mapping; outcome depends on how groups and target tokens are defined; English-centric.
implication: Bias can be detected as an asymmetric quality/accuracy gap, aligning model fairness with measured capacity rather than sentiment.
relevance: Provides an accuracy-gap methodology for detecting whether early-exit/adaptive LLMs give different prediction quality to different groups.

title: Quantifying Fairness in LLMs Beyond Tokens: A Semantic and Statistical Perspective
abstract: Proposes augmented fairness metrics at the semantic level (output meaning/similarity) combined with statistical group comparisons, arguing token- and word-level metrics miss semantic disparities in generated content.
oneLiner: Adds semantic-level fairness metrics on top of token/statistical metrics to surface group disparities token measures miss.
keyFinding: Token- and probability-level metrics understate semantic-level differences across groups, so fair-by-token models can still be semantically uneven.
weakness: Relies on semantic-similarity/embedding machinery that can be noisy; group definitions are user-chosen.
implication: Fairness evaluation needs semantic-level measurement; apparent token-level parity can mask unequal meaning quality across groups.
relevance: Provides semantic/metric machinery to test whether early-exit LLMs preserve meaning-quality parity across groups, not just token parity.

title: All Should Be Equal in the Eyes of Language Models: Counterfactually Aware Fair Text Generation
abstract: Proposes a counterfactually aware framework for fair text generation: generate counterfactual (group-swapped) inputs and use them to regularize the model so outputs are equally likely and semantically consistent across demographic attributes.
oneLiner: Uses counterfactual group-swapping to make generation equally likely and meaning-preserving across demographic groups.
keyFinding: Counterfactually aware regularization reduces demographic bias while maintaining generation quality and fluency.
weakness: Counterfactual generation limited to salient attributes; requires controllable generation and can distort rare/dependent attributes.
implication: Counterfactual fairness is an achievable target via data/objective engineering, feasible without harming quality much.
relevance: Defines a counterfactual-fairness target that early-exit LLMs should ideally preserve, to test whether adaptive inference breaks counterfactual invariance.

title: The Impact of Debiasing on the Performance of Language Models in Downstream Tasks is Underestimated
abstract: Evaluates the true downstream cost of common debiasing methods using broader and more robust performance evaluation, showing the performance/robustness loss from debiasing is larger than standard evaluations report.
oneLiner: Shows that standard debiasing methods hurt downstream performance and robustness more than earlier narrow-task evaluations suggest.
keyFinding: Measured across a broad task suite with robustness awareness, debiasing degrades downstream generalization and robustness substantially more than prior claims.
weakness: Focuses on intrinsic-to-extrinsic transfer and named debiasing methods; generalization to generative/RLHF-style LLMs limited.
implication: Debiasing is not free: removing bias can reduce quality/capability, so fairness and capability must be jointly optimized.
relevance: Frames the fairness-vs-capability trade-off that adaptive/early-exit inference also faces: budgeted compute may buy fairness or capability, sometimes at each other's expense.

title: Selecting Shots for Demographic Fairness in Few-Shot Learning with Large Language Models
abstract: Studies how the composition and selection of in-context examples (shots) in few-shot LLM learning affects downstream demographic fairness, proposing strategies to select demographically balanced demonstrations.
oneLiner: Shows the demographic makeup of in-context examples drives downstream group fairness and that balanced-shot selection helps.
keyFinding: The demographic distribution of selected shots strongly shapes fairness outcomes; selecting balanced shots improves fairness without significantly hurting accuracy.
weakness: Limited to few-shot in-context learning and a specific set of attributes/tasks; shot-selection search cost.
implication: Inference-time composition of the prompt — analogous to how adaptive inference composes computation — is a controllable lever on group fairness.
relevance: Shows inference-time composition (by analogy, early-exit/budget decisions) is a fairness lever, informing whether adaptive LLMs can be tuned to keep groups equal.

title: Pruning has a disparate impact on model accuracy
abstract: Shows that standard magnitude-based pruning degrades accuracy far more severely for minority/underrepresented groups than for majority groups, so compression introduces or amplifies group disparity; proposes a constrained pruning formulation.
oneLiner: Magnitude pruning disproportionately hurts minority subgroups' accuracy, so the compressed model is less fair than its dense counterpart.
keyFinding: Aggressive pruning produces unequal accuracy loss across demographics, with underrepresented groups bearing a larger drop, even when overall (average) accuracy is preserved.
weakness: Vision classifiers and a single pruning heuristic; accuracy-parity metric; mitigation adds optimization cost.
implication: An efficiency transform that looks 'fair' on mean accuracy can be systematically unfair to minority groups, so compression must be audited per-group.
relevance: Directly the closest analog to early-exit LLMs: an efficiency transform preserving average quality but redistributing error onto minority groups, motivating subgroup-level auditing of dynamic exits.

title: A Fair Loss Function for Network Pruning
abstract: Introduces a fairness-aware loss added during pruning so the pruned network does not diverge in performance across demographic groups, reporting balanced AUC-ROC across skin tones even under heavy pruning.
oneLiner: Adding a fairness loss during pruning keeps accuracy balanced across skin tones instead of letting AUC-ROC drift apart.
keyFinding: Pruning alone causes divergent AUC-ROC across dark vs light skin tones; a fair pruning loss eliminates that divergence while preserving sparsity.
weakness: Face/skin-tone centric; fairness term is a heuristic loss weight; narrow classifier and dataset.
implication: The pruning objective itself is the correct place to inject fairness, rather than post-hoc rebalancing of the sparse model.
relevance: Encapsulates how to make an efficiency transform fairness-aware during the compression step — analogous to making an early-exit policy fairness-aware at training time.

title: Coupling Fairness and Pruning in a Single Run: a Bi-level Optimization Perspective
abstract: Formulates fairness-preserving pruning as a bi-level optimization that jointly decides which weights to drop and enforces a fairness constraint (e.g., equalized odds), asking how to make a compressed model fair in one run.
oneLiner: Pruning and fairness are solved together as a single bi-level problem, so the sparse model satisfies both sparsity and group-fairness goals.
keyFinding: Treating fairness as a constraint inside a bi-level optimization lets pruning reach high sparsity without sacrificing equalized-odds across groups, outperforming post-hoc pruning-then-rebalancing.
weakness: Optimization more expensive and hyperparameter-sensitive; uses standard fairness benchmarks instead of LLM/foundation-model settings.
implication: Compression and fairness should be co-optimized, not sequential, because pruning first and correcting later tends to entrench disparity.
relevance: Provides the optimization machinery to add a demographic-fairness constraint when training early-exit heads, rather than auditing exits after the fact.

title: FairGRAPE: Fairness-aware GRAdient Pruning mEthod for Face Attribute Classification
abstract: Proposes a gradient-based pruning criterion that is fairness-aware for face attribute classification, so pruning keeps accuracy balanced across demographic groups while reducing computation.
oneLiner: A fairness-aware gradient-pruning criterion prunes networks for face attributes without worsening demographic imbalance.
keyFinding: Using a fairness-aware ranking of gradients (rather than plain magnitude) preserves demographic parity and individual fairness while pruning.
weakness: Face-specific; limited to attribute classification and one fairness metric; assumes well-annotated group labels.
implication: The criterion by which weights are pruned is itself a fairness lever; blind magnitude pruning can select the weights that protect minority groups.
relevance: Demonstrates that the pruning criterion — the analogue of an early-exit confidence rule — can be tuned to protect minority groups.

title: Balancing Act: Constraining Disparate Impact in Sparse Models
abstract: Develops a method to enforce sparsity and a disparate-impact (fairness) constraint simultaneously, producing sparse models that are both compact and fair, with a principled framework to trade off sparsity vs fairness.
oneLiner: Sparsity and disparate-impact constraints are enforced together, giving sparse models that stay fair by construction.
keyFinding: One can attain high sparsity while holding disparate impact near the pre-pruning level, but there is a real sparsity-versus-fairness trade-off a joint method navigates far better than post-hoc corrections.
weakness: Constrained optimization adds cost; benchmark-centered; guarantee depends on reliable group labels.
implication: Sparse-model fairness must be a hard constraint during training/compression, not an afterthought, and comes at a measurable sparsity cost.
relevance: Introduces the trade-off framing essential for early-exit LLMs: each exit threshold is a compression knob tunable against a fairness constraint.

title: Fair Scratch Tickets: Finding Fair Sparse Networks without Weight Training
abstract: Extends the lottery-ticket hypothesis to fairness, searching for fair sparse subnetworks ('fair scratch tickets') that are both accurate and fair without weight training, using a fairness-aware weight importance.
oneLiner: Fair, sparse winning tickets exist and can be identified in one shot without training, when importance is scored by a fairness-aware criterion.
keyFinding: Iterative magnitude pruning using a fairness-aware importance score finds sparse subnetworks that preserve (or improve) fairness while retaining accuracy.
weakness: Dataset/domain specific (image classification); fairness depends on the chosen importance metric and annotation; no large-transformer scaling.
implication: Fairness can be embedded in the selection of a sparse subnetwork at initialization, so compression need not be a fairness tax if the right subnetwork is chosen.
relevance: Shows a sparse-subnetwork (compressed) model can be fair by construction at initialization, analogous to choosing a fair early-exit subnetwork.

title: You Never Know: Quantization Induces Inconsistent Biases in Vision-Language Foundation Models
abstract: Systematically studies how quantization affects bias in multimodal vision-language foundation models, finding its impact is neither consistent nor uniform across models, tasks, and precision; some settings amplify bias, others reduce it.
oneLiner: Quantization's effect on multimodal bias is inconsistent across models and precision, so it cannot be assumed harmful or harmless.
keyFinding: Quantization-induced bias changes vary in direction and magnitude across vision-language models and bit-widths, so no single 'quantization hurts fairness' claim holds.
weakness: Multimodal scope; bias measured with a limited set of social-bias benchmarks; no consistent predictive rule.
implication: Fairness audits of quantized foundation models must be per-model and per-precision, since aggregate assumptions mislead.
relevance: Strongly parallels early-exit LLM fairness: the same efficiency transform changes bias in complex, non-obvious ways across models.

title: How Quantization Shapes Bias in Large Language Models
abstract: This work comprehensively evaluates how quantization affects model bias, with attention to individual demographic subgroups. Focusing on weight and activation quantization strategies, it examines effects across a broad range of bias types — stereotypes, fairness, toxicity, sentiment — using both probability- and generated-text-based metrics across 13 benchmarks and models differing in architecture family and reasoning ability. Findings: quantization has a nuanced impact on bias — it can reduce toxicity and does not significantly affect sentiment, but tends to slightly increase stereotypes and unfairness in generative tasks, especially under aggressive compression. Trends are generally consistent across demographic categories/subgroups and model types, though magnitude depends on the specific setting.
oneLiner: Quantization slightly increases stereotype/unfairness in generation while reducing toxicity, to varying degree by subgroup and setting.
keyFinding: Aggressive quantization tends to increase stereotypes and unfairness in generative tasks, with subgroup- and model-dependent magnitudes; toxicity can decline.
weakness: Reports average trends but notes magnitude varies by setting; does not isolate a mechanism; no early-exit/depth dimension; descriptive rather than causal.
implication: Establishes that compression redistributes bias onto (generative) fairness dimensions, and that per-subgroup effects are real and heterogeneous.
relevance: A. Broad empirical grounding for compression-induced subgroup bias; complements the mechanistic papers.
whyLatest: In-window (Aug 2025). Broad, benchmark-rich quantification of compression's effect on subgroup bias.
novelty: Broadest quantitative sweep of quantization→bias across 13 benchmarks, multiple bias types, and per-subgroup breakdown, using both probability- and generated-text metrics.

title: Fair-GPTQ: Bias-Aware Quantization for Large Language Models
abstract: The high memory demands of generative LLMs motivate quantization, which reduces memory by mapping weights to lower-precision integers. Recent empirical work shows quantization can increase the likelihood of biased outputs and degrade fairness benchmarks. This work links quantization and fairness by adding explicit group-fairness constraints to the quantization objective and introduces Fair-GPTQ, the first quantization method explicitly designed to reduce unfairness in LLMs. The added constraints guide the rounding operation toward less-biased text generation for protected groups, focusing on stereotype generation involving occupational bias and discriminatory language across gender, race, and religion. Fair-GPTQ has minimal accuracy impact (retains at least 90% of baseline accuracy on zero-shot benchmarks), reduces unfairness relative to a half-precision model, and preserves the memory/speed benefits of 4-bit quantization.
oneLiner: Adding fairness constraints to the quantization objective reduces bias with minimal accuracy loss.
keyFinding: Fair-GPTQ reduces unfairness vs. a half-precision model while retaining >=90% zero-shot accuracy and 4-bit memory/speed benefits.
weakness: Focuses on stereotype/occupational/discriminatory language (narrow bias types); no depth/early-exit dimension; accuracy-preservation floor of 90% is loose; limited model scale.
implication: Shows compression-induced unfairness is controllable at the objective level — a template for fairness-aware depth budgets in d3.
relevance: A-1 (core). Concrete compression-side fairness mitigation that d3 should port to the depth/exit budget.
whyLatest: In-window (Sep 2025). Provides the fairness-constrained compression method that d3's trade-off curve needs.
novelty: First quantization method with explicit group-fairness constraints in the quantization objective (bias-aware rounding) for LLMs.

title: Explaining How Quantization Disparately Skews a Model
abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) is widely used for its high compression capacity, speed, and minimal accuracy impact. However, the authors observe that disparate impact is exacerbated by quantization, especially for minority groups. They explain that a chain of factors in forward and backward passes creates disparate impact across groups: changes in weights and activations from quantization cause cascaded network effects, lowering logit variance, increasing loss, and compromising group accuracies. They extend the study to the influence on group gradient norms and Hessian eigenvalues from an optimization perspective. To mitigate, they propose integrating mixed-precision quantization-aware training (QAT) with dataset sampling and weighted loss functions, enabling fairer deployment of quantized networks.
oneLiner: Quantization cascades through the network to lower logit variance and worsen minority-group accuracy.
keyFinding: Quantization-induced changes to weights/activations cascade to lower logit variance, higher loss, and compromised group accuracy, particularly for minority groups; mitigable via mixed-precision QAT + reweighting.
weakness: Image/classification-oriented analysis; no open-ended generation or LLM benchmark; mechanism is optimization-theoretic, not evaluated on demographic LLM fairness datasets.
implication: Provides the causal mechanism (logit-variance collapse) that d3 predicts also operates in depth-budgeted/early-exit inference.
relevance: A-1 (core mechanism). The mechanistic backbone for d3; directly targestabishes the 'shared mechanism' hypothesis.
whyLatest: In-window (Sep 2025). Gives the mechanistic explanation d3 needs for how compression redistributes error.
novelty: Explains the disparate impact of quantization through a forward/backward causal chain (logit variance, loss, group accuracy, gradient norms, Hessian eigenvalues) and proposes a mixed-precision QAT + reweighting mitigation.

title: RELIANT: Fair Knowledge Distillation for Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Introduces a fairness-aware knowledge distillation approach for graph neural networks so the distilled (smaller) student stays fair even when the teacher is biased, balancing performance, complexity, and fairness.
oneLiner: A distillation loss that propagates fairness to a compact student, keeping compressed students group-fair.
keyFinding: Naive distillation inherits (and can amplify) teacher bias; adding a fairness-aware distillation objective yields fair, compact students without much accuracy loss.
weakness: Graph/transductive domain; requires an available teacher; fairness measured on graph node attributes.
implication: Distillation — a model-reduction transform — is a vector for bias transfer, so the student objective must explicitly enforce fairness.
relevance: Mirrors the teacher→student bias-transfer question for early-exit nets, where small exit heads distill the backbone's behavior (and biases).

title: What Is Left After Distillation? How Knowledge Transfer Impacts Fairness and Bias
abstract: Empirically studies how knowledge distillation affects fairness and bias, showing distillation can substantially change (and sometimes amplify) bias depending on teacher, student, and training setup; questions the assumption distillation is fairness-neutral.
oneLiner: Distillation is not fairness-neutral — it can amplify or reduce bias depending on teacher/student and settings.
keyFinding: Distilling a teacher into a smaller student shifts bias meaningfully, and the direction depends on distillation hyperparameters, teacher bias, and student capacity.
weakness: Descriptive, benchmark-driven; bias metrics are limited proxies; no corrective method proposed.
implication: Model reduction via distillation must be audited for fairness, because the smaller model can carry more (not less) bias than the teacher.
relevance: Directly relevant: exit heads effectively distill the backbone's outputs, so their bias must be audited separately.

title: Characterising Bias in Compressed Models
abstract: Examines how compression (pruning, quantization, distillation) interacts with fairness, showing that compressed models can disproportionately degrade underrepresented groups and that the effect is a function of the compression technique and group.
oneLiner: Compression does not affect all groups equally, so compressed models can be less fair than the originals.
keyFinding: Distillation and pruning at aggressive rates disproportionately hurt underrepresented groups even when average performance is maintained, and the bias depends on the compression method.
weakness: Focuses on standard compression methods and a set of benchmarks; group definitions and bias metrics limit scope.
implication: Compression is a fairness risk even when it preserves mean accuracy, so subgroup-level auditing is required for any model-reduction technique.
relevance: Foundational evidence that efficiency transforms (the class early-exit belongs to) can be fairness-detrimental, motivating group-level auditing.

title: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks: Temperature Scaling
abstract: Shows that modern neural networks are typically overconfident and miscalibrated, and introduces temperature scaling — a simple post-hoc transform of logits that markedly improves calibration.
oneLiner: Introduces temperature scaling as a simple, effective post-hoc calibration method for modern neural nets.
keyFinding: Modern networks are overconfident (poor ECE), and a single temperature parameter learned on validation data substantially recalibrates them, better than Platt or binning in many settings.
weakness: Post-hoc on validation data; a single global temperature is not group- or input-conditional; assumes a well-defined label distribution.
implication: Confidence scores are systematically miscalibrated, so any threshold on confidence (e.g., early exit) inherits that miscalibration.
relevance: Grounds the calibration-disparity mechanism: if temperature/confidence reliability differs across groups, a shared exit threshold exits at different true-error levels.

title: Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation in LLMs
abstract: Empirically evaluates how well LLMs can express uncertainty (verbalized confidence, sampling-based, verbalized-probability), finding significant overconfidence and poor failure prediction in vanilla confidence elicitation.
oneLiner: LLM verbalized confidence exhibits substantial overconfidence and poor failure prediction, casting doubt on its reliability.
keyFinding: Vanilla verbalized confidence is overconfident and unreliable for detecting wrong answers; certain prompting/self-consistency methods improve uncertainty estimation but not to a reliable degree.
weakness: Evaluates a limited set of elicitation strategies and tasks; confidence is not fully calibrated without post-processing.
implication: Since LLM confidence is unreliable, any confidence-driven early-exit decision has an uncertain basis, which could differ by input/group.
relevance: Directly supports the calibration-disparity hypothesis: if confidence reliability differs across groups, confidence-based early exit yields unequal quality.

title: Semantic Uncertainty: Linguistic Invariances for Uncertainty Estimation in Natural Language Generation
abstract: Introduces semantic entropy: cluster sampled generations by meaning (via entailment) and compute entropy over semantic equivalence classes, giving a way to estimate uncertainty in open-ended generation.
oneLiner: Aggregate sampling entropy over meaning-equivalent outputs to estimate generation uncertainty.
keyFinding: Semantic entropy better distinguishes correct from incorrect generations than token-level metrics, improving selective prediction and could reduce hallucination risk.
weakness: Requires multiple samples and an entailment model; relies on the meaning-partitioning assumption; cost is high.
implication: Token-level confidence is a poor proxy for generation uncertainty; meaning-aware uncertainty is more reliable.
relevance: If generation-uncertainty is meaning-based and differs across groups, then early-exit confidence (often token-level) may mis-rank groups.

title: Thermometer: Towards Universal Calibration for Large Language Models
abstract: Proposes a universal calibration method (Thermometer) that calibrates LLMs across tasks and input distributions using a small set of labeled data, addressing the task-specificity of temperature scaling.
oneLiner: A universal calibrator that works across tasks and distributions, avoiding per-task temperature tuning.
keyFinding: Thermometer generalizes temperature-scaling-style calibration across tasks, achieving better calibration with fewer labels and being robust to distribution shift.
weakness: Requires some labeled data; may not fully capture uncertainty in open-ended generation; calibration quality depends on calibration set.
implication: Calibration can be made task- and distribution-agnostic, but the calibration data composition (and any group skew) still matters.
relevance: Supports per-group calibrated confidence as a route to fair early-exit thresholds, and warns that calibration data must be representative.

title: Teaching Models to Express Their Uncertainty in Words
abstract: Trains a model (T5) to express uncertainty in words given a question and a set of sampled answers, so the model can verbalize calibrated-confidence answers.
oneLiner: Fine-tune a model to verbalize calibrated confidence about its sampled answers.
keyFinding: Trained verbalized confidence is better calibrated and more accurate than a baseline, improving calibration and selective prediction.
weakness: Requires sampled answers; verbalization is not fully reliable for very open tasks; not group-disaggregated.
implication: Confidence can be learned as a first-class output rather than derived from logits, offering a controllable uncertainty signal for exit decisions.
relevance: Suggests an alternative to raw logit confidence for early-exit decisions — a trainable, potentially group-calibrated signal.

title: Entropy Alone is Insufficient for Safe Selective Prediction in LLMs
abstract: Argues that entropy-based uncertainty is insufficient for safe selective prediction/abstention in LLMs, and that additional signals (e.g., semantic, self-consistency, calibration-aware) are needed.
oneLiner: Shows entropy is not a safe standalone signal for when LLMs should abstain or be trusted.
keyFinding: Low-entropy high-confidence outputs can still be wrong, so entropy alone is not a safe abstention/trust signal.
weakness: Entropy is a single-uncertainty proxy; findings depend on task and model; framing is empiricist.
implication: Early-exit decisions based purely on entropy (or confidence) may be unsafe, since low-uncertainty tokens can still be incorrect.
relevance: Warns that entropy thresholds (a common early-exit rule) are not sufficient to ensure quality parity across groups.

title: Revisiting Uncertainty Estimation and Calibration of Large Language Models
abstract: Re-examines uncertainty estimation and calibration for LLMs, comparing methods and finding that calibration and uncertainty-quality are model- and task-dependent, with implications for reliable confidence.
oneLiner: Reassesses LLM uncertainty/calibration across methods and models, showing dependency on model and task.
keyFinding: Uncertainty-estimation quality and calibration vary substantially across methods, models, and tasks, and are rarely reliable enough for risk-sensitive decisions.
weakness: Descriptive; relies on calibration/uncertainty proxies; limited corrective method.
implication: Portable, reliable confidence for LLMs remains unsolved, so decisions on confidence (e.g., early exit) need per-model auditing.
relevance: Underlines that exit-threshold confidence must be validated per model, task, and group to avoid unfair early-exit outcomes.

title: The Art of Abstention: Selective Prediction and Error Regularization for Natural Language Processing
abstract: Studies selective prediction (abstention) in NLP with a calibration-aware error-regularization training objective, improving the model's ability to abstain when uncertain and improving the risk-coverage trade-off.
oneLiner: A training objective that improves selective prediction (abstention) and the risk-coverage trade-off in NLP.
keyFinding: Error-regularized selective prediction substantially improves risk-coverage and calibration, enabling models to abstain on hard inputs while preserving accuracy on confident ones.
weakness: Focuses on classification-style NLP; abstention metrics may not map to generation; no group-level abstention analysis.
implication: Selective prediction gives a principled lever for compute-and-answer decisions; how well it abstains per group is a fairness question.
relevance: Provides the selective-prediction machinery to test whether a model abstains (exits) differently across demographic groups.

title: Calibrated Uncertainty Quantification for Multi-Modal LLMs
abstract: Studies calibrated uncertainty quantification for multimodal LLMs, showing that uncertainty methods calibrated on text-only LLMs do not transfer well and proposing calibration that accounts for modality.
oneLiner: Calibration tuned for text LLMs does not transfer to multimodal LLMs, so calibration must be modality-aware.
keyFinding: Uncertainty calibration methods from text-only LLMs transfer poorly to multimodal LLMs, and modality-aware calibration improves reliability.
weakness: Multimodal scope; relies on calibration/uncertainty proxies; limited model breadth.
implication: Calibration must be tailored to the model/modality and its input distribution, which can vary across content types.
relevance: Highlights that calibration (and thus early-exit confidence) is input-dependent, so different groups' inputs may be calibrated differently.

title: The Well-Tempered Classifier: Some Elementary Properties of Temperature Scaling
abstract: Study of the structural properties of temperature scaling, clarifying its role among calibration methods and its limitations, including conditions under which it is the only sensible post-hoc recalibration.
oneLiner: Analyzes temperature scaling's structural properties and its role/limits among calibration methods.
keyFinding: Temperature scaling is uniquely simple/robust among post-hoc calibrators, and its effectiveness is tied to assumptions about the label/score distribution that may not always hold.
weakness: Theoretical treatment with limited empirical breadth; assumes a well-defined score/label distribution.
implication: Temperature scaling is a convenient but assumption-laden calibrator; its single scalar cannot fix distribution- or group-specific miscalibration.
relevance: Reinforces that a single global temperature/exit threshold is insufficient for fair calibration across groups.

title: Beyond Post-Hoc Temperature Scaling: Bilevel Optimization for LLM Calibration
abstract: Proposes using bilevel optimization to calibrate LLMs, going beyond post-hoc temperature scaling by jointly optimizing the calibration with the model, improving calibration and robustness.
oneLiner: Calibrates LLMs via bilevel optimization, going beyond simple post-hoc temperature scaling.
keyFinding: Bilevel-optimized calibration outperforms post-hoc temperature scaling in calibration error and robustness, while integrating with preference-based training.
weakness: Optimization cost/complexity; evaluation on calibration proxies; limited breadth of models/tasks.
implication: Calibration can be integrated into training rather than applied post-hoc, enabling more precise (potentially group-aware) calibration.
relevance: Suggests a path to train fairness- and calibration-aware early-exit heads rather than post-hoc adjusting thresholds.

title: BERT Rediscovers the Classical NLP Pipeline
abstract: Probes each layer of BERT with lightweight classifiers for syntactic and semantic tasks, showing representations encode information in a pipeline-like bottom-up order.
oneLiner: BERT's layers recapitulate the classical NLP pipeline, with syntax emerging early and semantics later.
keyFinding: Per-layer probing accuracy organizes into a clear bottom-up order (surface → syntactic → semantic), each task peaking at a characteristic depth and often declining afterward.
weakness: Linear probes are read-only and show only what is decodable, not what the model uses; limited to BERT-base and English.
implication: Representation 'maturity' is task- and depth-specific, so a fixed-depth readout (including an early exit) captures different information for different inputs.
relevance: Supports the premise that layers reach probe-decodable ('mature') representations at different depths, the mechanism behind group-dependent early-exit gaps.

title: The Bottom-up Evolution of Representations in the Transformer: A Study with Machine Translation and Language Modeling Objectives
abstract: Studies how representations evolve layer by layer in Transformer MT/LM models, finding different types of linguistic information become separable at different depths and lower layers are more general while deeper are task-specific.
oneLiner: Transformer representations specialize bottom-up, with each type of linguistic knowledge emerging at a distinct layer.
keyFinding: Lower layers encode language-general features that transfer across objectives, while deeper layers encode task-specific information; specialization is incremental and bottom-up.
weakness: Focused on MT/LM objectives; relies on correlational probing and layer transfer.
implication: The 'maturity depth' of a representation depends on the information type, so shallow outputs retain general structure but miss deep task-specific signal.
relevance: Core evidence that the content of representations — and hence their maturity — unfolds across depth, enabling depth-dependent group differences.

title: Understanding Deep Neural Networks via Linear Separability of Hidden Layers
abstract: Proposes understanding deep neural networks by measuring the linear separability of representations at each hidden layer, showing how separability grows with depth and relates to accuracy.
oneLiner: Hidden representations become linearly separable as depth increases, yielding a quantitative 'maturity' measure per layer.
keyFinding: Linear separability of hidden representations increases progressively with depth and correlates with task accuracy, offering a layer-wise maturity metric.
weakness: Evaluated primarily on vision/feedforward architectures rather than Transformer LLMs; separability is dataset-specific.
implication: Separability is a computable, quantitative proxy for representation maturity that can be measured per subpopulation.
relevance: Supplies the operationalization of 'maturity' (linear separability / probe accuracy) to compare across demographic groups at different depths.

title: Investigating Gender Bias in BERT
abstract: Measures how gender information is distributed across BERT's layers by probing each layer for gender and stereotypical associations, localizing where bias is strongest.
oneLiner: Gender information is concentrated in particular BERT layers, and layer-wise probing localizes where stereotypes live.
keyFinding: Gender bias is unevenly distributed across layers; a subset of layers is far more predictive of gender and stereotype associations, i.e., the bias 'matures' at specific depths.
weakness: Encoder-only BERT, English, single demographic axis; probing is correlational and task-limited.
implication: If gender is decodable mainly at specific layers, then the depth at which inference stops directly changes the amount of gender information available.
relevance: Core evidence that a demographic attribute's representation becomes separable (mature) only at certain depths, implying group-specific fairness effects at early-exit cutoffs.

title: Locating and Mitigating Gender Bias in Large Language Models
abstract: Uses activation/influence analysis to locate which layers and modules in LLMs are responsible for gender bias, then mitigates it with targeted interventions.
oneLiner: Gender bias is localized to specific layers and components, so it can be targeted rather than treated uniformly.
keyFinding: Gender bias concentrates in particular layers and modules (often MLPs and attention at certain depths); removing it there reduces bias with minimal general-performance loss.
weakness: Bias measurement is attribute/task-dependent; mitigation heuristics may not generalize across all bias types.
implication: The depth at which outputs are taken changes the effective bias level, so early-exit depth selection is a fairness lever.
relevance: Directly ties layer depth to demographic-bias magnitude, the axis along which early-exit fairness gaps could emerge.

title: Projective Methods for Mitigating Gender Bias in Pre-trained Language Models
abstract: Examines how a gender subspace appears across the layers of pretrained LMs and compares projective methods that remove it, quantifying layer-wise bias strength.
oneLiner: A gender subspace recurs across layers with varying strength, and projecting it out has layer-dependent effects.
keyFinding: The feminine/masculine direction strength varies by layer (typically growing with depth), and projective debiasing behaves differently at different layers.
weakness: Focus on the gender subspace in BERT-class encoder models; bias measured via a single-direction projection.
implication: Since gender-direction strength is layer-dependent, exit depth directly affects how much gender information leaks into predictions.
relevance: Shows demographic (gender) signal strength is layer-dependent — matching the notion that groups' representations reach maturity at different depths.

title: Gender Encoding Patterns in Pretrained Language Model Representations
abstract: Probes how much gender information is encoded in pretrained LM representations and how this varies across layers and contexts.
oneLiner: Gender information is encoded unevenly across layers and contexts, revealing where demographic signals live.
keyFinding: The degree of gender encoding varies substantially across layers and depends on context, so no single layer is a uniform 'gender' source.
weakness: Recent preprint with narrower gender scope and limited model coverage; probing-based (correlational).
implication: Layer-dependent gender encoding means the information available at an early-exit depth differs across contexts and groups.
relevance: Supports the premise that demographic-attribute representations mature at different depths, manifesting as group-dependent early-exit accuracy.

title: Fine-Tuned Transformers Show Clusters of Similar Representations Across Layers
abstract: Measures representational similarity (CKA-style) between all pairs of layers in fine-tuned BERT-like models, revealing that layers organize into clusters of similar representations.
oneLiner: Transformer layers collapse into a few clusters of similar representations after fine-tuning, not a smooth gradient.
keyFinding: Fine-tuned layers show block/clustered similarity structure (early, middle, late groups), so representation change is not monotonic and some layer groups are near-redundant.
weakness: Focuses on representational similarity rather than task/attribute accuracy; encoder models only.
implication: If layers form near-redundant clusters, exit-depth choice and per-group maturity differences depend on cluster boundaries.
relevance: Characterizes how representations reorganize with depth, helping predict at which depth a group's information becomes (or stops being) separable.

title: On the Effect of Dropping Layers of Pre-trained Transformer Models
abstract: Investigates how much performance degrades when dropping individual (or groups of) layers from pretrained transformers, showing that not all layers contribute equally.
oneLiner: Some transformer layers are nearly redundant or even harmful, so layer removal is surprisingly cheap.
keyFinding: Many layers (including middle and some early ones) can be removed with minimal accuracy loss, revealing differential per-layer contribution.
weakness: Layer removal is a crude proxy for early exit; not tested for subpopulation fairness; encoder-heavy.
implication: Since layer importance varies, the depth at which inference stops does not preserve information equally across inputs.
relevance: Establishes that information is distributed unevenly across layers, so the layer at which inference exits determines what (and whose) information is preserved.

title: The Linear Representation Hypothesis and the Geometry of Large Language Models
abstract: Formally studies the linear representation hypothesis — that LLMs store features as directions in activation space — and analyzes the geometry of these representations.
oneLiner: LLM features are stored as linear directions, giving a geometric basis for reading concepts from hidden states.
keyFinding: Provides formal conditions and evidence that concepts are represented as approximately linear directions in activation space, supporting linear probing and steering.
weakness: Theory-oriented with limited empirical breadth; no direct per-layer maturity or demographic subgroup analysis.
implication: If concepts are linear directions, a linear probe at a layer measures how 'mature' a concept's direction is there.
relevance: Grounds the assumption that linear probing at a layer quantifies demographic-concept maturity, enabling depth-by-depth comparison of group representation maturity.

title: A Survey of Early Exit Deep Neural Networks in NLP
oneLiner: Reviews early-exit methods for NLP models (encoder and decoder), including exit criteria (confidence, entropy, patience, hash), multi-exit architectures, training schemes (self-distillation, layer dropout), and efficiency/quality trade-offs, with a focus on NLP tasks and emerging LLM settings.
keyFinding: Reviews early-exit methods for NLP models (encoder and decoder), including exit criteria (confidence, entropy, patience, hash), multi-exit architectures, training schemes (self-distillation, layer dropout), and efficiency/quality trade-offs, with a focus on NLP tasks and emerging LLM settings.
surveyScope: Reviews early-exit methods for NLP models (encoder and decoder), including exit criteria (confidence, entropy, patience, hash), multi-exit architectures, training schemes (self-distillation, layer dropout), and efficiency/quality trade-offs, with a focus on NLP tasks and emerging LLM settings.

title: Adaptive Inference through Early-Exit Networks: Design, Challenges and Directions
oneLiner: Foundational survey of early-exit (adaptive inference) networks: where exits are placed, how the decision to exit is made, how accuracy and latency trade off, and the open design challenges and research directions.
