title: Improving Group Fairness in Knowledge Distillation via Laplace Approximation of Early Exits
abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) trains compact student models from larger teachers. Because students learn simpler surface-level features in early layers, errors grow for groups whose labels spuriously correlate with input attributes, degrading group fairness even when overall accuracy is comparable. Early-Exit Neural Networks (EENNs) enable predictions at multiple intermediate layers; confidence margins from early exits have been used to reweight cross-entropy and distillation losses per instance. This paper proposes using Laplace-approximation-based, well-calibrated uncertainty estimates (rather than margins) to reweight hard/ambiguous instances and improve group fairness. They benchmark a BERT-based model on MultiNLI.
oneLiner: Calibrated uncertainty extracted at early exits can be used to reweight training and improve group fairness in distillation.
keyFinding: Laplace-based calibrated uncertainty at early exits more robustly identifies difficult/ambiguous instances than margin-based approaches, improving group fairness on MultiNLI.
weakness: Small scale (BERT on one multi-label benchmark), evaluates group fairness only via reweighting-driven accuracy, and does not measure per-group exit-depth/accuracy-vs-depth distributions under a fixed threshold.
implication: Suggests the exit-confidence signal is a legitimate fairness lever, motivating d1/d2: if calibration at exits is already used to improve fairness, a shared threshold may not exit at equal true-error across groups.
relevance: A-1 (core). Directly establishes early-exit + group fairness as connected, giving d1 a concrete anchor and confirming the mechanism (calibrated exit signal) that d2 formalizes.
whyLatest: Probably the single closest prior work to d1's exact question. Within ~1 year of the window (May 2025); a cornerstone for the intersection even though slightly before the strict 1-yr cutoff.
novelty: Uses Bayesian (Laplace) calibrated uncertainty from intermediate exits as a reweighting signal for fairness, positioning calibration of the exit signal as a fairness lever rather than a margins heuristic.

title: Beyond Greedy Exits: Improved Early Exit Decisions for Risk Control and Reliability
abstract: Early-Exit Deep Neural Networks allow adaptive inference by predicting at intermediate layers, cutting cost and latency. Most strategies greedily exit when confidence exceeds a threshold fixed on a static validation set, which is problematic because the model can be overconfident in a wrong class and is not robust to distribution shift. The authors propose UAT, which adapts the exit threshold online with a Multi-Armed Bandit framework, using a reward function that assesses predictive certainty and its reliability to balance efficiency and quality while penalizing unnecessary late exits. They provide risk guarantees and validate on vision-language understanding, text generation, and classification, achieving 1.70-2.10x speedup with <2% accuracy drop.
oneLiner: A bandit-based adaptive exit threshold improves reliability and speedup but keeps risk marginal rather than group-wise.
keyFinding: Adaptive, uncertainty-aware exit (UAT) yields 1.70-2.10x speedup with <2% drop and stronger risk control than static-threshold greedy exits.
weakness: Focuses on reliability/risk and efficiency, not demographic groups; no per-group fairness analysis; risk guarantees are marginal, not per-group (so a group-gap could persist by construction).
implication: Exit decision is a dynamic per-instance function; if the confidence signal is group-correlated, the adaptive threshold inherits that — an open door for d1/d2.
relevance: B. Useful as the current best model of the exit decision; supplies the mechanism and baseline that d1 must extend with per-group auditing.
whyLatest: In-window (Sep 2025). Directly about how exit thresholds are chosen — the very object d1 asks whether it treats groups differently.
novelty: Replaces static thresholds with an online, uncertainty-aware bandit that trades efficiency vs. reliability, and provides theoretical risk guarantees.

title: The Diminishing Returns of Early-Exit Decoding in Modern LLMs
abstract: In LLM inference, early-exit stops computation at an intermediate layer once the prediction is sufficiently confident, reducing latency and cost. But modern LLMs use improved pretraining recipes and architectures that reduce layer redundancy, potentially limiting early-exit opportunities. The authors re-evaluate layer-wise early-exit in modern LLMs, analyze how intermediate representations evolve during training, introduce a metric for intrinsic early-exit suitability, and propose a benchmark for exploring early-exit benefits on different models/workloads. They find a diminishing trend in early-exit effectiveness across newer generations; dense transformers generally offer more early-exit potential than Mixture-of-Experts and State Space Models; larger (>20B) and base pretrained models show higher early-exit potential.
oneLiner: Modern LLMs show diminishing and architecture-dependent early-exit potential.
keyFinding: Early-exit usefulness is shrinking in newer models and depends on architecture (dense > MoE/SSM), scale (>20B) and tuning (base > tuned).
weakness: Efficiency/suitability only — no fairness dimension; no per-group exit-depth or accuracy-vs-depth curves; ignores demographic stratification.
implication: Any d1 fairness result is conditional on the model's early-exit suitability; a fairness gap may be negligible simply because the model rarely exits early.
relevance: B. Sets the feasibility condition for d1 and warns that a small measured fairness effect may be an artifact of low early-exit potential.
whyLatest: In-window (Mar 2026). Grounds d1 by showing early-exit potential is model- and architecture-dependent, so any group bias will be model-specific.
novelty: Introduces a quantitative intrinsic early-exit-suitability metric and a comparative benchmark; explains diminishing returns via layer-redundancy reduction.

title: SimLens for Early Exit in Large Language Models: Eliciting Accurate Latent Predictions with One More Token
abstract: Intermediate-layer predictions in LLMs are informative but hard to decode accurately, especially at early layers. Lens-style methods typically use a direct linear readout that drifts from the model's eventual prediction. SimLens is a training-free decoder for single-token decision tasks that keeps only the start token and a candidate answer token and runs one lightweight continuation through the upper layers, recovering far more accurate latent predictions than direct linear decoding. Linear SimLens approximates entropy-based confidence, and SimExit combines both into a hybrid early-exit mechanism. On ARC, BoolQ, and HeadQA with LLaMA-7B/Vicuna-7B, SimLens improves Iso-Compute accuracy in all six settings (+0.43 average); SimExit yields 1.15x speedup at best-accuracy and 1.40x with up to 1-point accuracy drop.
oneLiner: A training-free decoder yields accurate intermediate-layer predictions and an entropy-based confidence signal for early exit.
keyFinding: SimLens recovers accurate intermediate predictions and improves Iso-Compute accuracy; SimExit gives ~1.15-1.40x speedup at controlled accuracy.
weakness: Single-token decision tasks only; no demographic/group analysis; no per-group exit-depth audit; assumes a single shared Iso-Compute benchmark.
implication: The exit signal (entropy/confidence) is now well-defined and accurate enough for d1 to compute per-group accuracy-vs-depth curves on it.
relevance: B. Methodological enabler for d1 (and d2) rather than a fairness result; good baseline for the accuracy-vs-depth measurement.
whyLatest: Jul 2025 (just at window edge). Demonstrates the modern confidence/exit estimation machinery in LLMs.
novelty: Training-free 'one more token' continuation decoder to recover accurate latent predictions; linear approximation of entropy for confidence; hybrid exit.

title: HALF: Harm-Aware LLM Fairness Evaluation Aligned with Deployment
abstract: LLMs are increasingly deployed in high-impact domains (clinical, legal, hiring, education), making pre-deployment fairness/bias evaluation critical. Existing evaluations are not grounded in real scenarios and ignore harm-severity differences (e.g., a biased surgical decision should not be weighted like a stylistic summarization bias). HALF (Harm-Aware LLM Fairness) assesses model bias in realistic applications and weighs outcomes by harm severity, organizing nine application domains into three tiers (Severe/Moderate/Mild) via a five-stage pipeline. Across eight LLMs, they find (1) LLMs are not consistently fair across domains, (2) model size/performance do not guarantee fairness, and (3) reasoning models do better in medical decision support but worse in education.
oneLiner: A deployment-aligned, harm-weighted framework shows LLM fairness is uneven across domains and not guaranteed by scale.
keyFinding: Fairness is domain-contingent and not guaranteed by model size/performance; reasoning models vary by domain (good in medical, worse in education).
weakness: No adaptive-inference/depth dimension; not about exit-depth or per-group compute; harm weighting is opinion-derived and domain-level not group-level.
implication: For d1, per-group fairness of adaptive compute must be assessed within deployment context and by harm severity, not just aggregate metrics.
relevance: B. Supplies the deployment-aware fairness lens and benchmark scaffolding for d1 without addressing adaptive compute itself.
whyLatest: In-window (Oct 2025). Supplies the fairness-evaluation framing for d1's per-group quality question.
novelty: Harm-severity-weighted, deployment-domain-aligned fairness evaluation with a three-tier harm taxonomy and staged pipeline.

title: Token-Level Entropy Reveals Demographic Disparities in Large Language Models
abstract: A name alone measurably reshapes a model's next-token distribution before any token is sampled. The authors measure full-vocabulary Shannon entropy of the next-token distribution across six open-weight model families on 5,760 sentence-completion prompts where race/gender are signaled only by a first name. Black-associated names co-occur with higher first-token entropy and more diverse continuations than White-associated names — directionally consistent in all six instruction-tuned models under shared raw-text input, all six base checkpoints, and (for output diversity) five of six models under native chat formatting — opposite to the homogeneity bias seen under explicit group labels. The gap persists under tokenization/frequency controls and on a frequency-matched subset; per-prompt effects are small (d=0.06-0.16) but uniformly signed (template-level paired d=0.66-1.08). Gender points the other way, additively with race. First-token entropy attenuates sharply under chat formatting, and explicit group-label probing is mostly null/reversed; a variance-matched comparison locates the output-diversity disparity in heterogeneity across name-conditioned continuations.
oneLiner: LLM token-entropy is already differentiated by signaled race/gender, so a confidence-gated exit threshold may exit differently across groups.
keyFinding: Black-associated names yield higher first-token entropy/diversity than White ones (uniformly signed across models), whereas explicit label probing is mostly null/reversed.
weakness: Sentence-completion entropy only; not tied to any early-exit/adaptive-compute policy; small per-prompt effects; no calibration/ECE analysis; chat-format dependence complicates generalization.
implication: If entropy gates early exit (CALM/PABEE-style), a single shared threshold will not yield equal exit-depth or equal true-error across groups — the d2 hypothesis.
relevance: A-1 (core, foundational). The empirical premise for d2 and the signal behind d1's exit decision.
whyLatest: Foundation for d2 (Jan 2025). Establishes that the exit-driving signal (next-token entropy) varies by signaled demographic group.
novelty: Shows a demographic disparity in the entropy of the token distribution itself, independent of explicit group labels, and shows probing methodology determines whether/which direction a disparity is detected.

title: The Confidence Trap: Gender Bias and Predictive Certainty in LLMs
abstract: As LLMs enter sensitive domains, how their confidence scores relate to fairness/bias matters. This study examines alignment between LLM-predicted confidence and human-annotated bias judgments, focusing on gender bias in gendered-pronoun-resolution contexts. It evaluates whether probability-confidence calibration metrics capture fairness-related disparities. Among six state-of-the-art models, Gemma-2 shows the worst calibration on the gender-bias benchmark. The main contribution is a fairness-aware evaluation of LLM confidence calibration plus a new calibration metric, Gender-ECE, designed to measure gender disparities in resolution tasks.
oneLiner: A fairness-aware calibration metric (Gender-ECE) reveals that model confidence is group-miscalibrated on gender bias.
keyFinding: Models differ sharply in gender calibration; Gemma-2 is worst; raw confidence calibration does not reflect gender fairness.
weakness: Gendered-pronoun resolution only (binary gender, a narrow task); six models; no mitigation/intervention; not tied to an adaptive-exit confidence policy.
implication: Shared confidence thresholds are group-miscalibrated on a protected dimension, amplifying the risk that adaptive-exit decisions discriminate.
relevance: A-1 (core). Supplies the measurement instrument and an empirical existence proof for group-wise confidence miscalibration.
whyLatest: In-window (Jan 2026). Introduces a group-conditional calibration metric exactly for d2's question.
novelty: Introduces Gender-ECE, a group-specific expected-calibration-error metric, and evaluates confidence-vs-bias alignment across six models.

title: Hierarchical Group-Conditional Conformal Risk Control for Selective Prediction in Language Models
abstract: LLMs serve heterogeneous populations structured by domain, topic difficulty, and linguistic style. Conformal risk control (CRC) gives rigorous marginal risk guarantees for selective prediction with abstention, but marginal guarantees do not imply per-group ones: a model can meet the population budget while systematically over-exposing subgroups to errors. Under mild shifts in group composition, standard CRC violates the budget in up to 47% of trials. HG-CRC (Hierarchical Group-Conditional CRC) is a post-hoc calibration framework enforcing simultaneous risk guarantees across all nodes of a user-defined group hierarchy, using a Bonferroni correction over nodes and a leaf-first policy that uses the most specific applicable threshold, backing off to coarser nodes when a finer one is uncertified or rejects the example. It needs only a held-out calibration set, no retraining. Evaluated on Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Gemma-3-4B over ARC Challenge and MMLU-Pro across eight configurations (IID, heterogeneity, mixture/domain/prompt/difficulty shift, label noise, quantization), HG-CRC reaches an empirical 0% violation rate and WGER=0 on ARC for high-accuracy models; results are benchmark-specific (MMLU-Pro models abstain entirely or retain WGER=0.014). Participation cost vs. global CRC is 22-37 points. Ablations show hierarchical depth clears the budget (removing difficulty level returns violations to ~11%); Bonferroni is needed for the guarantee though its empirical effect matters only with many nodes.
oneLiner: Hierarchical group-conditional conformal risk control enforces per-group risk guarantees on selective prediction with abstention.
keyFinding: HG-CRC reaches ~0% per-group violation (empirically) on ARC for well-calibrated models while standard CRC violates the budget in up to 47% of shifted trials.
weakness: Marginal-guarantee-forcing (not fairness-in-parity); high participation/coverage cost (22-37 points); still benchmark-specific; abstraction can trigger heavy abstention; not demographic-labeled fairness per se.
implication: Provides a concrete, testable mechanism for d2: group-conditional thresholding/calibration can flatten per-group error while preserving group safety.
relevance: A-1 (core/method). Provides the group-conditional calibration machinery d2 needs, and exposes its main cost (coverage).
whyLatest: In-window (Jul 2026). The most direct existing answer to d2's group-conditional calibration question.
novelty: Hierarchical group-conditional conformal risk control enforcing simultaneous per-group guarantees via Bonferroni + leaf-first threshold selection, post-hoc and calibration-only.

title: Fair and Calibrated Toxicity Detection with Robust Training and Abstention
abstract: Fairness in toxicity classification spans three integrated axes: ranking, calibration, and abstention. Training-time interventions and post-hoc safety mechanisms cannot be evaluated independently because the former determines the latter's efficacy. The authors compare ERM, instance-level reweighting, and Group DRO across these axes, combined with temperature scaling, confidence-based abstention, and per-identity threshold optimization. Evaluation uses subgroup AUC, BPSN/BNSP AUC, error gaps, and per-subgroup ECE with bootstrap CIs (n=1000). Findings: (1) calibration disparity is a hidden fairness violation — ERM has near-perfect aggregate calibration (0.013) but is miscalibrated across all identity subgroups (+0.029 to +0.134); (2) training interventions reshape rather than eliminate disparity (reweighted ERM improves ranking but worsens the calibration-fairness gap by up to +0.232; Group DRO removes calibration disparity only by becoming uniformly miscalibrated, ECE 0.118); (3) post-hoc methods inherit training failure modes (temperature scaling fails because miscalibration is non-uniform; confidence abstention works under ERM but breaks under DRO where the risk-coverage curve rises with deferral); (4) abstention itself is unfair — confidence-based deferral helps background content far more than identity-mentioning content.
oneLiner: Calibration disparity is a hidden fairness violation, and confidence-based abstention can be unfair across groups.
keyFinding: Aggregate calibration can look perfect (ECE 0.013) while all subgroups are miscalibrated; temperature scaling fails on non-uniform miscalibration; confidence abstention underperforms for identity-mentioning content.
weakness: Toxicity classification (not generation); per-identity rather than broad demographic groups; abstention is a yes/no safety decision, not a depth decision; small-scale.
implication: For d2, both per-group calibration AND the abstention/exit decision itself can carry group bias — a shared exit threshold is doubly at risk.
relevance: A. Empirically demonstrates group-wise calibration disparity and the group-unfairness of abstention — core evidence for d2.
whyLatest: In-window (May 2026). Provides per-subgroup ECE and shows temperature scaling + abstention behave differently across groups.
novelty: Jointly evaluates ranking, calibration, and abstention with per-subgroup ECE; shows training interventions reshape (not remove) calibration disparity and that abstention is itself group-unfair.

title: Density Ridge Selective Prediction for LLM and VLM Hallucination Detection under Calibration Label Scarcity
abstract: Hallucination detection is increasingly framed as selective prediction: an estimator scores confidence and abstains when low. Unsupervised sampling detectors (Semantic Entropy) avoid labels but plateau in quality, while supervised probes are strong in-distribution but degrade under calibration-label scarcity. The authors recover the response manifold as the density ridge of a kernel density estimate over a six-dimensional kinematic feature map of hidden-state generation trajectories, scoring a test generation by the negated Euclidean distance from its projected point to the nearest ridge vertex. Against Semantic Entropy, topological methods, and log-probability on six QA benchmarks (HaluEval-QA, TriviaQA, GSM8K, POPE, ScienceQA, A-OKVQA) with eight text/vision LLMs under a label-scarce protocol (n_cal=200, N=5 generations), the ridge score beats on AUROC by 5-20 points with tempered degradation under label scarcity.
oneLiner: A density-ridge confidence estimator is more accurate but still degrades under calibration-label scarcity.
keyFinding: Density-ridge scoring beats Semantic Entropy/log-probability by 5-20 AUROC points and degrades more gracefully under label scarcity (n_cal=200).
weakness: No fairness/group dimension; hallucination-detection framing; no per-group calibration or demographic analysis; geometric estimator is domain-specific.
implication: Per-group calibration for small demographic groups will face label scarcity; this work shows which estimator degrades least and how much.
relevance: B. Methodological complement for d2 (confidence estimation under scarce calibration data) but with no fairness dimension.
whyLatest: In-window (Jun 2026). Provides a state-of-the-art selective-prediction/confidence estimator and a scarcity analysis that d2's per-group calibration must handle.
novelty: Density-ridge geometric skeleton of the output distribution for confidence estimation; label-scarce selective prediction.

title: Uncertainty Drives Social Bias Changes in Quantized Large Language Models
abstract: Post-training quantization cuts cost but fundamentally alters social biases in ways aggregate metrics miss. The authors present the first large-scale study of 50 quantized models on PostTrainingBiasBench, a unified benchmark of 13 closed- and open-ended bias datasets. They identify 'quantization-induced masked bias flipping', where up to 21% of responses flip between biased and unbiased states after quantization despite no change in aggregate bias scores. Flips are strongly driven by model uncertainty: high-uncertainty responses are 3-11x more likely to change than confident ones. Quantization strength amplifies this — 4-bit models show 4-6x more behavioral change than 8-bit. Critically, changes create asymmetric impacts across demographic groups, where bias can worsen by up to 18.6% for some groups while improving by 14.1% for others, yielding misleadingly neutral aggregate outcomes. Larger models show no consistent robustness advantage, and group-specific shifts vary unpredictably across model families.
oneLiner: Quantization flips biases unpredictably and asymmetrically across groups, driven by uncertainty, even when aggregate bias is unchanged.
keyFinding: Up to 21% of responses flip bias state with no aggregate change; uncertainty makes flips 3-11x more likely; asymmetric group impacts (+18.6% worse / -14.1% better) cancel in aggregate.
weakness: Quantization-specific (not pruning/early-exit); uncertainty link is correlational; group-specific shifts vary unpredictably across models, limiting portability of conclusions.
implication: The uncertainty/confidence signal is the driver of compression-induced, group-asymmetric error — directly bridging d3 to d2 and to d1's entropy-gated exit.
relevance: A-1 (core, bridging). Jointly supports d3 (compression redistributes to groups) and d2 (uncertainty drives it), implying depth-budgeted inference will also redistribute via uncertainty.
whyLatest: In-window (Feb 2026). Most direct evidence that uncertainty drives group-asymmetric bias redististribution under compression — the d3/d2 bridge.
novelty: Defines 'quantization-induced masked bias flipping'; ties it to model uncertainty; shows group-asymmetric (18.6% worse / 14.1% better) shifts that net to neutral in aggregate.

title: The Impact of Inference Acceleration on Bias of LLMs
abstract: LLMs are large and costly/slow to run, so a body of work proposes inference-efficiency strategies — quantization, pruning, and caching — that cut cost/latency by several factors while retaining much of benchmark accuracy. This work explores another performance dimension: demographic bias in model generations due to inference-acceleration optimizations. Using a wide range of metrics, they probe bias from many angles. Analysis before/after acceleration shows significant change in bias. Worryingly, these bias effects are complex and unpredictable: a given acceleration-strategy × bias-type combination may show little change in one model but a large effect in another. The results highlight a need for case-by-case evaluation of model bias after acceleration changes.
oneLiner: Inference acceleration changes LLM bias in complex, model- and strategy-specific ways.
keyFinding: Acceleration optimizations cause significant, unpredictable changes in demographic bias; effects vary by strategy-model-bias-type combination.
weakness: Older (outside strict window); observable-level and unpredictable; no mechanistic explanation; no per-group exit-depth or depth-budget analysis; acceleration strategies treated at a high level.
implication: Adopting acceleration (including adaptive-depth) without per-group re-audit risks silent bias shifts — the practical motivation for d3 and d1.
relevance: A-1 (foundational, slightly older). The anchor reference for d3's 'compression/efficiency redistributes bias' framing.
whyLatest: Foundation for d3 (Oct 2024). Across ~18 months but is a cornerstone of the compression→bias literature the plan builds on.
novelty: Systematically evaluates how inference-acceleration strategies (not just accuracy) alter demographic bias, and shows the effects are strategy/model-specific and unpredictable.
